snippet.title: K-Pop Demon Hunters: Why It Took 7 Years (And a Big Twist) to Finish
snippet.description:
Seven years, countless rewrites, and one game-changing twist—this is how K-Pop Demon Hunters became a global Netflix phenomenon.

K-Pop Demon Hunters: The 7-Year Journey Explained. The animated sensation wasn’t an overnight hit—it was years in the making, with a bold creative pivot that redefined the project.

Director Maggie Kang spent seven years shaping the story of HuntRix and the Saja Boys, balancing supernatural folklore with the vibrancy of modern K-pop. Early drafts leaned heavily on demon-hunting action, but the “big twist” came when music moved from the background to the forefront, driving the plot and character arcs. With song-first storyboarding, frame-accurate syncing, and inspiration from groups like BTS, BLACKPINK, and Stray Kids, every performance became its own cinematic event.

But the challenges weren’t just creative. Sony hesitated, while Netflix jumped in with a $100M+ commitment that transformed the project into a global hit. The result? A record-shattering release with hundreds of millions of views, a surprise theatrical sing-along event, and a passionate worldwide fanbase.
Now, with a sequel on the horizon, K-DAH is set to expand its world, explore new genres, and continue proving that culturally specific stories can resonate everywhere. This is the untold journey of how a seven-year dream became a global phenomenon.

snippet.title: Ron Howard’s Eden: The Secret That Dictated Every Shot
snippet.description:
Production designer Michelle McGahey takes us behind the scenes of Ron Howard’s long-awaited passion project Eden. In this exclusive Collider interview, McGahey reveals how she recreated the unforgiving landscapes of the Galápagos Islands without ever leaving Australia—capturing the grit, the heat, and the isolation that define Floriana.

McGahey discusses how her time on Easter Island informed the raw aesthetic, why Queensland’s microclimates became the perfect stand-in, and how her team built entire sets—including homes, boats, and cactus groves—in just five weeks. From the research into archival photos and journals to the painstaking work of aligning locations with the DP’s vision, every detail was designed to ground Eden in realism and texture.

She also shares stories of storms that threatened the shoot, the cast’s resilience under blistering heat, and the collaborative dynamic between Ron Howard, DP Mathias, and the Australian crew. It’s a rare look into how environment and history shape a film’s emotional core.

snippet.description:
Special effects lead Adam Johansen takes us behind the scenes of I Know What You Did Last Summer in an exclusive practical-effects breakdown—an Adam Johansen interview that digs into prosthetics, blood rigs, and the finishing work that makes every death feel real. 

Johansen traces the process from his early conversations with Jennifer about where to set the gore/realism line through on-set execution: testing a spear-gun gag with props and SFX, selecting camera-safe Dark Arts blood that pops under moody lighting, and building the Teddy & Grant tableau like a fishing-weigh-in. He explains how LA body scans moved into ZBrush, then into molds and silicone with detailed hair work—pulled off on a roughly seven-week clock. We also touch on Judah’s church reveal (why environmental storytelling matters) and how a single makeup-only hand sells Milo’s demise. Throughout, Johansen shows why bold staging only works when the finish holds up to a close-up.

snippet.title: The Gilded Age S3: Filming Inside Nearly $1B of Mansions
snippet.description:
The Gilded Age S3: Filming Inside Nearly $1B of Mansions
Step inside the real 19th-century locations behind HBO’s The Gilded Age: New York and Rhode Island streets, estates, and museum-grade mansions, guided by details straight from the production.

We track Season 3’s footprint from Troy, Schenectady, Albany, and select NYC/White Plains spots to Long Island’s Old Bethpage Village Restoration and Gold Coast Studios. In Rhode Island, filming stretched across Providence’s historic streets and Newport’s grand summer mansions. Production designer Bob Shaw reveals how a modern space was transformed into the Tenderloin nightclub using 19th-century Orientalist design, and how his team balances research with creativity. 

Mansion highlights include Marble House, The Elms, Rosecliff, and The Breakers—each playing a key role in bringing the Russells’ world to life. To protect these fragile sites, the crew uses meticulous preservation methods, sometimes even closing historic rooms to the public for weeks at a time.

snippet.description:
28 Year Later: Inside the Tricks That Make It So Scary | Collider BTS
Sound designer Johnnie Burn goes behind the scenes with Collider to reveal how the film’s audio was built to feel raw, animalistic, and immersive—sometimes by literally moving bodies in the booth, other times by blending human voices with coyote wails so you question what you’re hearing.

Burn explains why emotion leads the mix, how silence lets your imagination do the scaring, and why authenticity matters (“you can tell when it’s fake”). He shares the workshop process behind a pivotal guttural roar, ultimately performed by a death metal vocalist, and how the team layered coyotes, pigs, and even lions into the infected’s voices.

With no electricity or tech in the story world, the team recorded nature deep in quiet Welsh woods to build a Britain without traffic hum. Burn also recalls the “hanging man” scene recorded in a controlled booth with a plastic bag, and crafting the eerie Bone Temple atmosphere using wind instruments, flutes, and even scaffolding poles played “badly.” Finally, he breaks down the complex Causeway sequence, balancing threat, footsteps, and the chase of an “alpha” against the Ring Cycle’s “Valkyries.”
